forms.name: Claymation
forms.what: Figures of clay or plasticine, posed and photographed one frame at a time. Soft, lumpy, a little uneven, and never perfectly smooth in motion.
forms.origin: Plasticine dates from 1897. Art Clokey (Gumby) and Aardman, founded in 1972, made the look famous.
rules: Rounded volumes with small lumps and dents, never a perfect sphere
Matte, high-roughness surfaces under soft light
Saturated colour, few of them
Small asymmetries; a silhouette that changes slightly between poses
A miniature set: a floor, a backdrop, shallow depth
forms.timing: Shot on doubles: about 12 pose changes a second inside a 24 frames-a-second film. Each held pose sits a hair differently from the last.
build: Three.js: `MeshStandardMaterial` with roughness about 0.9, metalness 0, and a noise canvas as `bumpMap`
Push each vertex in or out by a few percent with a seeded hash, then `computeVertexNormals()`
Pose from stepped time: `held(t, 12)`
Add a seeded nudge per drawing to position and rotation (about 2% of the size)
A hemisphere light plus one soft key; no hard specular highlights
forms.assets: Geometry in code (spheres, capsules, lathes) for simple characters. Fingerprint or noise detail as a generated bump texture. A real character needs modelling.
forms.sound: Close foley on pose changes (soft thuds, squelches), light percussion. Practice note.
pitfalls: Smooth 24 or 30 frames-a-second motion: it reads as CG, not clay
forms.blender: Use Blender when the clay needs real subsurface scattering, soft area-light shadows or sculpted detail.

forms.name: Stop-motion look
forms.what: Any real object moved and photographed a pose at a time. On screen it shows as stepped motion, tiny position errors and light that flickers a little.
forms.origin: As old as film: stop tricks appear in the 1890s. Pixilation, cut-out and puppet animation are all forms of it.
rules: Real materials: wood, card, cloth, plastic
Position jitter of a pixel or two between drawings
Lighting that varies slightly frame to frame
Hard cuts between poses, no in-between blur
forms.timing: On twos (12 changes a second) is the usual cadence; action sometimes on ones, held moments on threes or more.
build: Quantise time before anything else: `const ts = held(t, 12)`
GSAP: `ease: "steps(12)"` on a one-second tween does the same for a tween
Jitter and flicker keyed to the frame number: `jit(frameOf(t, 12), i, 1.2)`
Keep the camera and background steady: step the subject, not the world
forms.assets: None needed. Everything is procedural.
forms.sound: Foley that lands on pose changes. A bed that is not too smooth. Practice note.
pitfalls: Stepping the camera and background together, so everything strobes
Easing between held poses, which defeats the look
Jitter so large the object vibrates

forms.name: Paper cut-out
forms.what: Flat shapes cut from paper or card, layered, and moved a pose at a time. Parts hinge at joints; nothing bends.
forms.origin: Lotte Reiniger's The Adventures of Prince Achmed (1926) is the oldest surviving animated feature. Terry Gilliam's Monty Python animations and the South Park pilot used cut paper.
rules: Flat fills with hard, slightly uneven cut edges
Layers stacked with a small, tight shadow under each
Rigid parts that rotate about a pivot
Paper grain over everything
A limited, slightly muted palette
forms.timing: Stop-motion cadence, usually on twos. Motion is rotation about joints and sliding, with pops and holds.
build: Each part is its own shape; nudge the corners with a seeded hash so edges look cut by hand
Canvas: `shadowOffsetY` 3 to 4 px with `shadowBlur` 4 to 5 px per layer. DOM: `filter: drop-shadow()`
Joints: rotate about a pivot (`transformOrigin` in GSAP, `translate` then `rotate` on a canvas)
Paper grain: a noise texture drawn once and laid over with `multiply`
SVG route: `feTurbulence` into `feDisplacementMap` (scale 2 to 4) roughens an edge
forms.assets: Shapes drawn in code or as SVG. Photo cut-outs need images you own, or generated ones.
forms.sound: Paper rustle, snips, soft ticks on pose changes. Practice note.
pitfalls: Smooth vector motion with no stepping
Large soft shadows, which look like interface cards, not paper
forms.blender: Use Blender for real folded paper with thickness and light passing through it.

forms.name: Felt and fabric craft
forms.what: Shapes that look needle-felted or sewn: a fuzzy edge of loose fibres, a matte mottled surface, visible stitches.
forms.origin: Needle felting tangles wool fibres with barbed needles to make flat pictures and soft figures.
rules: A halo of short fibres along every edge
Matte, slightly mottled colour
Stitches: a dashed line just inside the edge
Chunky, simple forms in wool colours
forms.timing: Stop-motion cadence, on twos. Gentle bobbing and nudging.
build: Draw the shape, then several hundred short strokes outward from its edge, each angled by a seeded hash
Stitches: `setLineDash([9, 7])` on a path just inside the edge (SVG: `stroke-dasharray`)
Mottle: a grain texture clipped to the shape with `multiply`
SVG route: high-frequency `feTurbulence` (0.8 to 1.2) with displacement scale 3 to 6 on the edge
forms.assets: Procedural. A felt texture from an image model helps for close-ups.
forms.sound: Soft, warm, acoustic. Practice note.
forms.blender: Use Blender hair or fur for real fibre fuzz on 3D figures.
forms.thin: The craft is well documented; its use in animation is a practice note, not sourced.

forms.name: Origami
forms.what: Paper folded from a flat sheet: sharp creases, flat facets, each fold a clean move followed by a pause.
forms.origin: Japanese paper folding. Modern computational origami works from crease patterns.
rules: Sharp mountain and valley creases
Flat facets, each shaded as one plane
Paper coloured on one side, white on the other
Soft, even light so the creases read
forms.timing: Folds are eased moves of about 0.8 seconds with a short hold after each. Smooth, not stepped.
build: 2D: a fold is a point travelling across the crease; draw the moving flap from the crease to that point
Shade the flap by its angle, and swap to the paper's other colour past 90 degrees
3D: flat-shaded polygons, child groups rotating about the crease axis
An orthographic camera gives a diagram-clean view
forms.assets: Geometry in code. A faint paper grain.
forms.sound: Light paper crinkle on each fold, soft piano or music box. Practice note.
pitfalls: Folding with no hold, so the eye cannot follow
forms.blender: Use Blender when the paper has to bend or show thickness.

forms.name: Shadow puppetry
forms.what: Flat figures held between a lamp and a cloth screen: dark silhouettes with punched patterns on a warm, glowing field.
forms.origin: An old tradition across Asia. Ravana Chhaya of Odisha uses uncoloured deerskin puppets with no joints; wayang kulit of Java and Bali was recognised by UNESCO in 2003. Lotte Reiniger brought silhouettes to film.
rules: Black silhouettes on a warm lit screen, never on white
Interior detail made of perforations: rows of holes and cut patterns
A lamp that flickers
The shadow softens and grows as the puppet moves away from the screen
Rods visible below the figures
forms.timing: Live puppets move continuously on rods; film versions are stop-motion, so use twos. Stiff, deliberate moves; no squash and stretch.
build: One path per puppet filled with the even-odd rule, so holes are part of the figure
Screen: a radial gradient from warm yellow to deep brown
Flicker: scale the lamp brightness by a seeded value per drawing
Distance from the screen: `filter: blur()` growing with distance, and lower opacity
Ravana Chhaya style: no joints, move and tilt the whole puppet. Wayang style: hinge the arms
forms.assets: Simple figures in code. Ornate traditional figures need drawing or tracing with care.
forms.sound: Narrator, singers and percussion in the tradition: cymbals and drums for Ravana Chhaya, gamelan for wayang.
pitfalls: Black on white, which loses the lamp
Careless drawings of sacred figures: check the iconography with a source
forms.blender: Use Blender for real light through translucent coloured leather.

forms.name: Collage and mixed media
forms.what: Pieces of different papers, photographs and print stuck together: mismatched scale and texture, torn edges, hard shadows.
forms.origin: From the French coller, to glue. Braque and Picasso brought it into modern art around 1912; Dada followed with photomontage.
rules: Torn or cut edges
Mixed materials: flat colour, halftone photograph, tape
Overlap with a hard, offset shadow
Mismatched scale on purpose
One palette holding it together
forms.timing: On twos or threes. Pieces pop into place on the beat with a small rotation, then hold.
build: Torn edge: walk the outline of a rectangle and nudge every point with a seeded hash
Hard shadow: `shadowBlur: 0` with an offset of 5 to 6 px
Halftone a photo: dots on a staggered grid sized by brightness
Entrance: scale from 1.25 to 1 with a quarter-turn of rotation over a quarter of a second
forms.assets: Paper textures in code. Photo fragments need images you own, or generated ones.
forms.sound: Bright percussive music, staccato effects on each pop. Practice note.
pitfalls: Too many unrelated colours and typefaces

forms.name: Risograph and halftone print
forms.what: The look of a cheap stencil print: two to four bright inks laid over each other, visible grain, dot screens, and layers that never quite line up.
forms.origin: The Risograph duplicator dates from 1980: one ink per drum, so each colour is a separate pass. Halftone dots go back to the 1860s.
rules: Two to four spot colours, often pink, blue and yellow
Inks overprint to make new colours (multiply)
Each layer sits a pixel or two off register
Grain and dot screens; no smooth gradients
Off-white paper
forms.timing: Print is still. Animate by re-rolling the misregistration and swapping the grain 8 to 12 times a second.
build: Each ink is its own layer drawn with `mix-blend-mode: multiply` (canvas: `globalCompositeOperation`)
Offset each layer by a seeded amount per drawing: `jit(frameOf(t, 8), layer, 3)`
Tone as dots: a staggered grid of circles whose radius follows the tone
Grain: several pre-made noise tiles, cycled by frame number
Three.js `HalftonePass` exists for 3D scenes; SVG `feColorMatrix` separates a photo into one ink
forms.assets: All procedural. A chunky sans or slab typeface.
forms.sound: Lo-fi, tape hiss. Practice note.

forms.name: Anime and cel shading
forms.what: Light broken into two or three flat tones with a hard edge between them, and an ink outline around every form.
forms.origin: Named after the celluloid sheets of hand-drawn animation. In 3D it became toon shading, as in Jet Set Radio and The Wind Waker.
rules: Two or three tone bands with hard edges
Shadows tinted with colour, not black
A clean outline
Flat, detailed backgrounds behind simpler characters
Limited animation: holds, then sudden moves
forms.timing: On twos as the baseline, ones for key action, threes and holds for dialogue.
build: Three.js `MeshToonMaterial` with a `gradientMap`: a three-texel `DataTexture` with `NearestFilter`, so light snaps to bands
Outline by inverted hull: a second copy of each mesh, slightly larger, drawn back faces only in black
`OutlineEffect` and `SobelOperatorShader` in the three.js examples are the two other routes
Step the pose time: `held(t, 12)`
2D: flat SVG shapes, a thick outline, `steps()` timing
forms.assets: The gradient map is three bytes. Characters need modelling or generated models.
forms.sound: Whoosh and impact effects on key poses. Practice note.
pitfalls: Smooth interpolation at 24 frames a second
Shadows that are only a darker grey
forms.blender: Use Blender for Freestyle line art and shader-to-RGB ramps on real characters.

forms.name: 2D flat vector explainer
forms.what: The plain explainer look: flat fills, a few colours, simple shapes and icons, smooth eased motion.
forms.origin: Flat design comes from Swiss style and modernism; in animation its ancestor is the stylised, limited look of the UPA studio.
rules: Flat fills, three to five colours, one accent
Geometric shapes with one stroke width
Plenty of space; one idea per frame
Clean sans type
forms.timing: Smooth ease-out moves of 0.4 to 0.8 seconds, staggered, with holds long enough to read.
build: HTML or SVG with GSAP: this is what HyperFrames is best at
Stagger related items 0.15 to 0.25 seconds apart
Draw check marks and connectors on with `stroke-dashoffset`
Move a highlight instead of cutting
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: Soft interface blips, a light bed, voice-led pacing. Practice note.
pitfalls: Too much on screen at once

forms.name: Whiteboard and doodle
forms.what: Marker lines that draw themselves on a white board, in the order someone would draw them. The chalkboard is the same recipe, inverted.
forms.origin: Also called video scribing. A 2016 study found little evidence that it teaches better than other formats, so use it for its tone, not as a learning trick.
rules: Black marker lines with a slight wobble
Strokes appear in drawing order
One or two accent colours
Chalk variant: a dark board, dusty broken strokes, a little smudge
forms.timing: Each element draws on over 0.3 to 1.5 seconds, paced to the narration. The line boils at about 10 changes a second.
build: Draw-on: a polyline drawn up to a fraction of its length (SVG: `stroke-dashoffset`)
Boil: nudge every point by a seeded amount keyed to `frameOf(t, 10)`
Chalk: three thin passes of the same stroke with different dash patterns at half opacity, over a speckled board
rough.js (MIT) generates sketchy shapes and hatching to animate afterwards
forms.assets: All in code. A marker or chalk typeface if the system has one.
forms.sound: Marker squeak, voice-led. Practice note.
pitfalls: A hand that covers the drawing

forms.name: Watercolour
forms.what: Transparent washes on textured paper: colour that spreads, pools darker at its edge, and lets the paper show through.
forms.origin: Pigment in water on paper. Wet-on-wet blends softly; wet-on-dry gives crisp edges.
rules: Transparent colour; overlaps make new colours
Darker pigment at the edge of each wash
Irregular, soft outlines
Paper grain visible everywhere
Unpainted paper as the highlight
forms.timing: Slow. A wash grows over 1 to 3 seconds with an ease-out. Hold drawings at 12 a second for a hand-painted feel.
build: Each wash: an irregular closed outline, clipped, filled with a radial gradient that is darkest near the rim
Layer washes with `multiply`
Paper grain over everything with `multiply`
SVG route: low-frequency `feTurbulence` (0.01 to 0.03) into `feDisplacementMap` (scale 10 to 25) for bleeding edges
3D: a Kuwahara filter as a custom pass gives a painterly result; three.js ships none
forms.assets: Procedural. A scanned paper texture improves close-ups.
forms.sound: Slow, gentle, acoustic. Practice note.
pitfalls: A uniform blur, which looks out of focus, not painted
forms.thin: The edge-darkening rule is a practice note; the technique sources cover the filter, not the look.

forms.name: Ink wash (sumi-e)
forms.what: Black ink in every shade from deep black to pale grey, laid down in tapered brush strokes on rice paper, with a great deal left empty.
forms.origin: Chinese ink wash painting from the Tang dynasty, carried to Japan by Zen monks. Shanghai Animation Film Studio made ink-wash films from 1960.
rules: One ink, many dilutions
Strokes that taper from thick to a point
Empty paper as part of the picture
One small red seal
Soft grey washes behind sharp strokes
forms.timing: Slow and fluid. A stroke accelerates and lifts. On twos.
build: A stroke is a row of overlapping dots whose radius tapers along its length, drawn up to a fraction
Vary each dot's opacity with a seeded hash for a dry-brush break
Washes: soft radial gradients with `multiply`
SVG route: variable-width filled paths revealed by a mask
forms.assets: Procedural. Rice-paper grain.
forms.sound: Sparse: flute, single plucked notes, silence. Practice note.

forms.name: Line art
forms.what: One weight of line on a plain ground, no shading: the drawing draws itself, then quivers slightly as if redrawn each frame.
forms.origin: Drawing with line alone, where tone comes only from hatching or stippling.
rules: A constant or tapered stroke with round ends
No fills, or one flat tone
Plenty of empty space
One accent colour at most
forms.timing: Draw-on over 1 to 2 seconds, then a boil at 8 to 12 changes a second.
build: Draw-on with `stroke-dashoffset` (canvas: a polyline to a fraction of its length)
Boil: a seeded nudge of 1 to 2 px per point, keyed to the frame number
SVG route: `feTurbulence` with `seed` set from the frame number, into `feDisplacementMap` (scale 1.5 to 3)
`vector-effect: non-scaling-stroke` keeps the weight when scaled
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: A pencil or pen sound under the draw-on. Practice note.
pitfalls: Jitter so strong the line turns to noise
Filters that re-run on a large area every frame and slow the render

forms.name: Rotoscope look
forms.what: Real movement traced by hand: lifelike motion, flat colour fields that drift, and an outline that shimmers.
forms.origin: Max Fleischer built the rotoscope. A Scanner Darkly, Waking Life and the a-ha video for Take On Me are the well-known examples.
rules: Motion with the timing of live action
Flat or posterised colour fields
Outlines that change slightly every drawing
Colour that sits a little off the line
forms.timing: Every frame or on twos. The boil is keyed to the drawing.
build: From footage: draw each video frame to a canvas, posterise it, find edges (three.js has `SobelOperatorShader`), then nudge the edges per drawing
From code: a figure built from joints, drawn twice: thick flat colour offset by a seeded amount, then a thin outline with its own nudge
Re-encode source video with a keyframe on every frame so seeking is exact
forms.assets: Footage you own, or a figure built in code.
forms.sound: The original scene audio, or music-led. Practice note.
pitfalls: Edge noise that flickers out of control
Losing the subject in the treatment
Tracing footage you have no right to use
forms.blender: Dedicated tools do true painterly rotoscoping better than a browser.

forms.name: Motion comic
forms.what: Comic panels brought to life: layers inside a panel slide at different speeds under a slow camera move, then a hard cut to the next panel.
forms.origin: Watchmen: Motion Comic (2008) is the usual first example.
rules: Ink outlines, flat colour, halftone shading
A panel border
Foreground, figure and background on separate layers
Bursts and lettering as graphic elements
forms.timing: Slow pushes and pans of 2 to 4 seconds, hard cuts between panels, a pop for a burst.
build: Layers in a clipped panel; move far layers less than near ones
A slow scale from 1 to about 1.07 on the whole panel
Halftone shading: dots that shrink across the tone
Cut to the next panel by switching the scene at a time, not by cross-fading
forms.assets: Drawn panels in layers. Artwork needs an illustrator or generated images cut into layers.
forms.sound: Voice, music and effects carry it. Practice note.
pitfalls: A slow zoom on one flat image, which reads as a slideshow
No separation between figure and background
forms.thin: Pan-and-zoom staging is a practice note; the source describes the format, not the technique.

forms.name: UPA and mid-century modern
forms.what: Flat, stylised design from 1950s cartoons: geometric characters, abstract backgrounds, colour printed slightly off its outline, and very few drawings.
forms.origin: United Productions of America turned away from Disney realism and made limited animation a style. Gerald McBoing-Boing won an Academy Award in 1950.
rules: Characters built from triangles, circles and lines
Flat colour blocks that do not meet their outlines
Abstract backgrounds: a few shapes, no perspective
A warm, muted palette
forms.timing: Limited animation: a pose is held, then pops to the next. Eight or fewer changes a second.
build: Flat shapes; draw the outline 6 to 9 px away from the fill
Two or three poses, switched on a frame count with no in-betweens
Paper grain with `multiply`
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: Jazz combo, sound effects as music. Practice note.

forms.name: Rubber-hose cartoon
forms.what: The 1920s cartoon: limbs like hoses with no elbows or knees, round bodies that bounce to the music, black and white film.
forms.origin: Credited to Bill Nolan on Felix the Cat. The Fleischer studio kept it longest; Cuphead revived it.
rules: Curved tubular limbs
Round forms
Black and white or sepia, high contrast
Film grain, scratches and a frame that weaves slightly
Everything moves to the beat
forms.timing: Bouncy loops locked to the music, on twos, with squash and stretch.
build: A limb is a quadratic curve between two points; move the control point to bend it
Squash and stretch: scale the body on one axis by the inverse of the other
Grain: cycle a few noise tiles by frame; gate weave: shift the whole picture by a seeded pixel or two
Sepia with `feColorMatrix` if wanted
forms.assets: All in code. Original characters only.
forms.sound: Hot jazz, slide whistles, effects on every bounce. Practice note.
pitfalls: Copying characters that are still under copyright

forms.name: Linocut and woodcut print
forms.what: A relief print: bold flat shapes in one to three inks, with white gouge marks where the block was carved.
forms.origin: Carved in linoleum or wood; the uncut surface prints. Each colour is a separate block.
rules: Bold shapes, no fine detail
Short white cut marks inside the ink, all leaning one way
One to three inks, laid slightly off register
Paper showing at the edges
forms.timing: Each colour arrives as a pull, top to bottom, then holds. On twos or slower.
build: Draw each block to its own canvas, then cut marks out of it: short strokes with `destination-out`
Print blocks over each other with `multiply`, the second one offset a few pixels
Reveal a block by widening a clip from the top
SVG route: `feTurbulence` through a hard threshold makes rough voids
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: A roller, a press, paper lifting. Practice note.
forms.thin: The source covers the technique; the visual rules are practice notes.

forms.name: Isometric
forms.what: A parallel projection seen from above at an angle: no perspective, three visible faces per block, a tidy model world.
forms.origin: A technical drawing projection. Games use a 2:1 pixel slope, about 26.6 degrees, which is strictly dimetric.
rules: No perspective: parallel lines stay parallel
Three tones per object: top lightest, one side mid, one side darkest
One light direction for everything
A grid floor
forms.timing: The camera does not orbit. Objects drop, stack and slide along the three axes, staggered by grid position.
build: 2D: `x = (gx - gy) * s`, `y = (gx + gy) * s / 2 - gz * s`; draw the two side faces, then the top
Sort by `gx + gy`, then by height, so nearer cubes cover farther ones
Three.js: an `OrthographicCamera` placed at equal x, y and z looking at the origin
CSS: `rotateX(60deg) rotateZ(-45deg)` on a flat layer
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: Soft clicks as pieces land. Practice note.
pitfalls: Shadows that disagree with the light
forms.blender: Use Blender for bevelled, ambient-occluded isometric scenes.

forms.name: Low-poly 3D
forms.what: Meshes with few polygons, each face lit as one flat facet. A hardware limit that became a style.
forms.origin: From the era of early 3D consoles; chosen on purpose since about 2013.
rules: Visible facets, flat shaded
A limited, saturated palette
Simple lighting and a gradient or flat sky
Chunky silhouettes
forms.timing: Clean, so smooth: slow eased orbits and dollies at the full frame rate.
build: Low segment counts and `flatShading: true` on `MeshStandardMaterial`
Displace a plane's vertices with a seeded hash for terrain, then `computeVertexNormals()`
A hemisphere light plus one directional key; fog in the sky colour for depth
Camera position from `t` directly
forms.assets: Geometry in code for landscapes and props. Characters need modelling.
forms.sound: Calm, spacious. Practice note.
pitfalls: Smooth normals, which erase the facets
Detailed textures that fight the flat colour
forms.blender: Use Blender for modelling and baked light.

forms.name: Voxel
forms.what: Everything built from cubes of one size on a grid, like a three-dimensional pixel picture.
forms.origin: A voxel is a value on a 3D grid. Minecraft made the look familiar.
rules: One cube size, integer positions
Each face one flat tone
A small palette
Small floating scenes
forms.timing: On twos. Things appear cube by cube or layer by layer; moves snap to the grid.
build: One `InstancedMesh` of a box for all the cubes: one draw call
Set each cube's matrix from stepped time; hide a cube by scaling it to nothing
Cubes slightly under size (0.96) so the seams read
`MeshLambertMaterial` and a hemisphere light
forms.assets: Models as arrays in code, or made with a voxel editor.
forms.sound: Blocky, percussive, chiptune. Practice note.
pitfalls: Faces flickering where cubes touch at full size

forms.name: Pixel art
forms.what: A tiny picture placed pixel by pixel and scaled up with hard edges: a few colours, no blur, sprites that step.
forms.origin: From early video games; the term dates from 1982.
rules: A small canvas scaled by a whole number
A limited palette, often 8 to 32 colours
No anti-aliasing, no soft gradients
Sprites animate in a few frames
forms.timing: Walk cycles of 4 to 8 frames at about 8 a second. Scrolling moves in whole pixels.
build: Draw on a small canvas (160 by 90), then `drawImage` it up with `imageSmoothingEnabled = false`
CSS: `image-rendering: pixelated` on an upscaled canvas
Sprites as arrays of palette indexes
Three.js: `RenderPixelatedPass` renders a 3D scene to low resolution with nearest filtering
forms.assets: Sprites as data in code, or drawn in a pixel editor.
forms.sound: Chiptune. Practice note.
pitfalls: Mixed pixel sizes on one screen
Smooth vector edges or too many colours

forms.name: 3D product render
forms.what: A studio shot of an object: a seamless backdrop, soft key, fill and rim lights, controlled reflections, a slow turn.
forms.origin: Product photography lighting, done in 3D.
rules: A seamless backdrop
Key light to one side and above, a softer fill opposite, a rim light behind
A contact shadow under the object
True materials: gloss, metal, glass
One slow move
forms.timing: Smooth and slow at the full frame rate. The opposite of the handmade looks.
build: `MeshPhysicalMaterial` with `clearcoat` for lacquer, `metalness: 1` for metal
Three directional lights in the key, fill and rim positions, plus a hemisphere light
Contact shadow: a plane with a radial-gradient texture, `depthWrite: false`
Rotation from `t` directly; ease the camera, not the turntable
forms.assets: A model of the product: built in code, made with the 3D pack, or supplied.
forms.sound: Minimal: a low bed and one accent on the reveal. Practice note.
pitfalls: No reflections, so it looks like plastic
An object floating with no shadow
forms.blender: Use Blender when the brief asks for photoreal glass, caustics or depth of field.
forms.thin: The lighting source is about photography; applying it to rendering is a practice note.

forms.name: Kinetic typography
forms.what: Moving words as the whole picture: scale, weight and timing carry the meaning.
forms.origin: Saul Bass's title sequences for North by Northwest (1959) and Psycho (1960) made it a form.
rules: Type is the image; nothing competes with it
Strong contrast of size and weight
Words arrive in reading order, on the beat
One idea per frame
forms.timing: Each word lands in 0.3 to 0.5 seconds with a small overshoot, then the line holds long enough to read.
build: HyperFrames: split text into inline-block spans and stagger with GSAP
Canvas: `fillText` with a transform per word
Timing from the narration: one start time per word
Hold for (words / 3) + 0.5 seconds before the next line
forms.assets: A typeface with enough weights. No pictures.
forms.sound: Cut to the voice or the beat. Practice note.
pitfalls: Words faster than they can be read

forms.name: Infographic and data animation
forms.what: A chart that builds in a sensible order: axes, then the data from an honest baseline, then the exact values.
forms.origin: From Playfair's first charts in 1786 to animated infographics in music videos in 2002.
rules: One chart type that fits the data
Direct labels, not a legend
An honest axis: bars start at zero
One colour for the point being made
forms.timing: Axes in about half a second, each series over 0.8 to 1.5 seconds with an ease-out, then a hold to read.
build: Drive the chart from one time value; never use a chart library's own transitions
Bars grow from the baseline; counters show the rounded value as it grows and end on the exact figure
SVG or canvas with scale maths; D3 scales are enough
Every number needs a source in the brief
forms.assets: The data, with its source.
forms.sound: A tick or tone per value, a bed that stays out of the way. Practice note.
pitfalls: An axis cut off to exaggerate a difference

forms.name: Lyric video
forms.what: The words of a song as the main image, each line timed to the vocal and the active word lit.
forms.origin: Lyric text appears in music videos from the 1980s; the format took off on video sites in the 2010s.
rules: Three to eight words on screen
The word being sung is brighter or larger
A background that never fights the text
One typographic system for the whole song
forms.timing: Locked to the music. A word changes exactly on its beat; a few frames late is visible.
build: Word start times from forced alignment or a beat grid
Compute the active line and word from `t`
A pulse from the beat phase: `1 - (beat % 1)` drives scale and background
Measure words first so the line is centred

forms.what: The damage of old tape and broken data: colour that bleeds sideways, scan lines, a band of noise at the bottom, sudden torn slices.
forms.origin: VHS records colour at far lower resolution than brightness, which is why colour smears. Glitch art uses such errors on purpose.
rules: Colour offset from brightness by a few pixels and softer
Scan lines
A tracking band of noise near the bottom
A date stamp in a blocky face

Chroma bleed: a blurred copy drawn again a few pixels to the side with `screen`
